name: SwiftFormat
verdict_reason: The only published head-to-head is NSHipster's 2019 timing of one small file: SwiftFormat 0.03 s, swift-format 0.24 s. That swift-format build used Swift 4.2's slowest way to get a syntax tree and has since moved to the Swift-native parser, and no current large-codebase comparison exists.
tier_reason: Independent third-party timing with hardware stated, but a single small file and 2019-era versions.
claimed_speedup: 0.03 s vs 0.24 s real time to format one example file (about 8x, derived from page data)
workload: Formatting a single short Swift example file with default settings, timed with time(1)
hardware: 2017 MacBook Pro, 2.9 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM
install: Homebrew, Mint, CocoaPods, Swift Package Manager plugin
one_liner: Swift code formatter with its own tokenizer; timed 8x faster than swift-format on one small file in 2019, unmeasured since.
how_it_is_fast: SwiftFormat uses its own lightweight tokenizer and applies rules to the token stream, rather than building a full syntax tree. In 2019 swift-format had to run swiftc and parse a large JSON file to get its tree, which dominated the timing.
use_it_when: Format-on-save or pre-commit hooks where per-file latency matters
Teams already standardized on SwiftFormat's rule set
skip_it_when: Choosing on speed alone today: the measured gap is from 2019 and swift-format's parser has since been rewritten
Projects that want the formatter shipped with the Swift toolchain (swift-format is included in Swift 6 toolchains)
caveats: One small file; process startup likely dominates both timings
2019 versions on an Intel MacBook Pro; swift-format then used Swift 4.2's slow SwiftSyntax path
No modern benchmark of either tool on a large codebase was found
tradeoffs: Its own parser can lag new Swift syntax compared with SwiftSyntax-based tools
Different default style and rule set from swift-format

evidence.quote: Timings are measured in seconds and taken on a 2017 MacBook Pro with 2.9 GHz Intel Core i7 processor and 16 GB 2133 MHz LPDDR3 memory.
SwiftFormat is consistently the fastest of the tools tested in this article, completing in a few milliseconds. $ time swiftformat Example.swift 0.03 real 0.01 user 0.01 sys
$ time swift-format Example.swift 0.24 real 0.16 user 0.14 sys
Our initial benchmarks reflected the Swift 4.2 version of SwiftSyntax, which predates these optimizations.
the NSHipster article compared swift-format using swift-4.2 which only provides the slowest available way to get a SwiftSyntax tree (invoke the swiftc binary and parse a large JSON file)
